query: Design a hypothesis to achieve coercive field ($H_c$) values exceeding 100 Oe in an fcc-based high-entropy alloy containing Ti. The operating regime of interest involves magnetic ordering temperatures significantly above room temperature. The known failure mode in existing single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni systems is a suppression of the orbital moment leading to low coercivity. Propose a design constraint involving the introduction of a secondary phase or specific chemical interaction that could alter the magnetic ground state or coupling without disrupting the fcc matrix, and describe a falsification experiment to distinguish between single-phase and dual-phase magnetic contributions.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a secondary phase of Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates (e.g., TiFe or TiNi) within an fcc Fe-Co-Ni high-entropy alloy matrix will induce a localized enhancement of the orbital magnetic moment at the phase boundaries via strain-induced symmetry breaking, thereby increasing the coercive field ($H_c$) to exceed 100 Oe while maintaining a Curie temperature ($T_C$) significantly above room temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni high-entropy alloy containing Ti, exhibiting suppressed orbital moment and low coercivity (<100 Oe) due to itinerant magnetism and high symmetry.
generation.intervention: Controlled thermal aging or rapid solidification to nucleate a coherent or semi-coherent secondary phase of Ti-rich intermetallics (e.g., B2 or L12 structure) within the fcc matrix without dissolving the primary phase.
generation.conditions: Operating temperatures between 300 K and 0.8 $T_C$; magnetic field cycling up to saturation; processing temperatures sufficient to drive phase separation but below the solvus of the fcc matrix.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent/semi-coherent phase boundaries creating local lattice strain fields that break cubic symmetry and lift orbital degeneracy.
generation.mechanism:
The strain field at the interface between the fcc matrix and the Ti-rich secondary phase reduces the local symmetry, enhancing the spin-orbit coupling strength and recovering the orbital magnetic moment ($L$), which increases the magnetocrystalline anisotropy energy ($K_1$) and consequently the coercivity ($H_c 
eq 2K_1/M_s$).
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit $H_c > 100$ Oe and a $T_C$ > 350 K, with X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) showing a significantly higher orbital-to-spin moment ratio ($L/S$) at the phase boundaries compared to the bulk single-phase material.
generation.baseline: The single-phase fcc Fe-Co-Ni-Ti alloy with $H_c < 100$ Oe and low $L/S$ ratio.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis fails if the secondary phase is incoherent (causing domain wall pinning rather than anisotropy enhancement) or if the phase separation temperature reduces $T_C$ below room temperature.
generation.uncertainty: Insufficient evidence to confirm the specific crystallographic structure of the Ti-rich precipitate or the exact magnitude of the orbital moment enhancement in this specific high-entropy system; the mechanism relies on theoretical extrapolation of strain effects on orbital moments in complex alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of samples: Set A (dual-phase) via aging to induce Ti-rich precipitates, and Set B (single-phase) via rapid quenching to suppress precipitation. Perform XMCD measurements at the Fe L-edge and Ti L-edge to quantify the orbital moment ($L$) and spin moment ($S$) separately, and measure $H_c$ via VSM.
measurements: Orbital moment ($L$) via XMCD sum rules
Spin moment ($S$) via XMCD sum rules
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Set A (dual-phase) shows no statistically significant increase in the $L/S$ ratio compared to Set B (single-phase) while $H_c$ remains < 100 Oe, or if $H_c$ increases in Set A but $L/S$ decreases, the hypothesis that orbital moment enhancement drives the coercivity increase is falsified.
